stances.claim: Work-from-home is not only feasible but already operationally proven for corporate governance during lockdown -- board and committee meetings via Zoom and Microsoft Teams can match the substantive deliberation of in-person meetings, with even per diems handled by direct bank credit.
stances.rhetorical_move: personal-witness validation (CJ's own First Philippine Holdings and Meralco board experiences) as proof-of-concept

stances.claim: Free videoconferencing platforms carry an under-appreciated data-ownership cost -- Zoom (free tier) owns the data of its users -- so corporate users handling sensitive matters should pay for platforms like Adobe Connect where the subscriber owns the data.
stances.rhetorical_move: expert-attribution (Judith Duavit Vazquez's warning) used to surface a privacy distinction lay readers miss

stances.claim: The judiciary cannot remain closed indefinitely under lockdown; while full trials require in-person observation of witness credibility, many judicial proceedings -- pretrial conferences, marking of exhibits, arguing ordinary motions, and especially appellate oral arguments -- can be conducted entirely via teleconferencing without violating any constitutional right of the accused.
stances.rhetorical_move: stage-by-stage segmentation of judicial proceedings to identify the digitally tractable subset

stances.claim: Appellate collegiate courts (Supreme Court, Court of Appeals, Sandiganbayan) are particularly well-suited for teleconferenced oral arguments because their work is dominated by written pleadings and parties seldom face each other physically anyway.
stances.rhetorical_move: court-tier differentiation (trial vs appellate) to make the strongest case at the top of the hierarchy

notable_anecdotes: The televised March 23 House Special Session -- conducted with only a handful of solons physically present in the Session Hall while the majority participated, voted, and tracked debate in real time from their homes via video and audio teleconferencing devices -- used as the column's working demonstration that WFH legislative work is already viable in the Philippines, even if 'quite primitively.'

CJ's family 'kumustahan' via free Zoom -- five children and ten grandchildren spread across Makati, Alabang, New York City, Greenwich, and Chicago all virtually reassembled -- offered as the warmest personal proof that the platform works across thousands of kilometers, with the editorial doubling as a snapshot of his transnational family during quarantine.

Judith Duavit Vazquez's caution that the free version of Zoom does not guarantee privacy 'as the platform owns the data of its users' -- surfacing a distinction between free and paid videoconferencing that most lay users in March 2020 had not yet learned to make.

The reform of corporate per diems being credited directly to directors' bank accounts instead of being issued as physical checks that had to be deposited in person -- a quiet operational dividend of pandemic-era WFH that CJ highlights as small but emblematic.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that the COVID-19 enhanced community quarantine, far from halting institutional life, is normalizing work-from-home arrangements that the Philippines should embrace and extend -- including, importantly, into the judiciary. He cites the March 23, 2020 House Special Session held with only a handful of solons physically present while the rest joined by video and audio teleconferencing, and his own experience as an independent director of First Philippine Holdings (using Zoom) and Meralco (using Microsoft Teams), where board and committee meetings ran smoothly with materials circulated by email in advance and even directors' per diems credited directly to bank accounts. He also recounts a family 'kumustahan' over free Zoom that reunited his five children and ten grandchildren spread across Makati, Alabang, New York City, Greenwich, and Chicago. He flags Judith Duavit Vazquez's warning that the free version of Zoom does not guarantee privacy because the platform owns user data, and contrasts this with paid platforms like Adobe Connect, used by US publicly listed companies, where the subscriber owns the data. He then argues that the judiciary must keep up with the digital age: while full trials require in-person observation of witness credibility and body language, many proceedings -- pretrial conferences, exhibit marking, ordinary motion arguments, and especially appellate oral arguments in the Supreme Court, Court of Appeals, and Sandiganbayan, which seldom involve face-to-face party encounters -- can readily be done by teleconferencing without violating any constitutional right.
